topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European digital public health contexts; competencies may differ in non-European healthcare systems with different regulatory, infrastructural, or policy environments. Findings are most directly applicable to EU/UK public health organisations.
takeaways: Use the framework to audit current AI literacy gaps in your public health workforce — identify which digital competencies are most critical for your organisation's priority areas (e.g., data analytics, AI tool evaluation, governance).

Prioritise foundational digital literacy and critical appraisal skills before advanced AI training, as these enable staff to evaluate and safely implement digital tools rather than passively consuming them.
Design role-specific competency pathways rather than one-size-fits-all training — public health practitioners, analysts, and leaders require different AI capabilities.

articles.title: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Developing a competency framework for artificial intelligence in undergraduate dental education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to dental education context. Findings may not generalise to other healthcare professions or non-clinical fields without adaptation. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: If developing AI literacy programs in professional education, use competency frameworks to define specific skills students should master rather than generic AI awareness training.
Consider sector-specific AI applications (e.g., diagnostic imaging, treatment planning in dentistry) when designing curricula, as competencies will differ from generic AI literacy programs.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Limited — the article focuses on Generation Z and educational strategies, but geographic scope and sector applicability are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Findings may vary significantly across different education systems and labour markets.
takeaways: Identify which AI literacy gaps are most pressing in your organisation's Gen Z cohort (e.g., foundational concepts vs. tool proficiency) and design targeted upskilling programs accordingly rather than generic AI awareness training.

Consider embedding innovative educational strategies such as project-based learning, real-world problem-solving, and cross-functional collaboration into your employee development programs to build sustained AI capability rather than one-off training sessions.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development would require significant adaptation.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-technical learners works best when embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught as an isolated skill — consider how AI competencies connect to data literacy, critical thinking, and digital citizenship in your training design.

Middle school frameworks emphasize foundational conceptual understanding over technical skills — this suggests adult employees may benefit from similar scaffolding that builds conceptual mental models of AI before moving to tool-specific applications.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development; generalisability to other sectors and disciplines unclear without access to full article.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is common but addressable through structured development programs that build confidence and competence before expecting implementation.
Designing AI literacy initiatives for educators first (rather than jumping to student training) creates multiplier effects — faculty then model and teach AI capabilities more effectively.
Consider staged development: move from awareness-building to hands-on practice with real tools, with psychological safety and low-stakes experimentation built in.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — presents a theoretical model for higher education institutions, but lacks empirical validation across diverse institutional types, geographies, or sectors beyond academia.
takeaways: Consider adopting a multi-domain AI literacy framework (likely encompassing technical, ethical, organisational, and strategic dimensions) rather than treating AI skills as standalone technical competencies—this meta-skill approach may better prepare academic leaders for institutional change.

The model suggests AI literacy should be integrated into management development and leadership programmes in universities; assess whether your organisation's learning initiatives address all four domains or focus narrowly on tool use.

Use this framework to map gaps in your team's AI capabilities across domains and design targeted upskilling interventions that connect AI understanding to organisational strategy and decision-making, not just technical proficiency.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet. Findings on job crafting responses to AI adoption may vary across industries, organisational contexts, and employee demographics.
takeaways: Employees exhibit different job crafting responses to AI adoption — some proactively reshape their roles (approach behaviour) while others withdraw or avoid new AI-integrated tasks (avoidance behaviour). Understanding these patterns helps managers identify who needs targeted support during AI implementation.

Use an approach-avoidance lens when designing AI change management: some employees need reassurance and capability-building to engage with AI, while others need clarification about how AI enhances rather than replaces their work.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings on psychological ownership and AI crafting may have limited generalisability outside paternalistic leadership contexts, which are more prevalent in some Asian cultures. Applicability to egalitarian or distributed leadership models common in Western organisations requires further investigation.
takeaways: Cultivate psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in AI customisation and configuration decisions — this sense of ownership drives more effective human-AI collaboration than top-down AI implementation.

In paternalistic leadership environments, leaders can leverage their trusted position to guide employees toward AI crafting behaviours (tailoring AI systems to their workflows), which bridges the gap between technological capability and actual adoption.

When implementing AI, prioritise opportunities for employees to shape how AI tools work in their roles rather than treating AI as a fixed, pre-configured system — this agency strengthens both collaboration quality and likely reduces resistance.

articles.title: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI usage and employee creativity: the mediating role of work engagement and the moderating role of technology acceptance  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The proposed mediation and moderation model may apply broadly to knowledge-work settings, but effectiveness likely varies by industry, organisation type, and employee demographics. Geographic scope unclear.
takeaways: Work engagement appears to be a key mechanism linking AI tool adoption to creative output — focus on maintaining or boosting engagement when introducing AI to protect creative capability.

Technology acceptance (user attitudes and perceived usefulness of AI tools) moderates the relationship — invest in change management and usability training to ensure employees see AI as genuinely helpful, not threatening to their creative role.
Simply rolling out AI tools without attention to engagement levels or user buy-in may not unlock the creativity benefits organisations expect.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — unable to assess sample size, geography, or sector from the title and excerpt provided. Recommend reviewing full article for methodological details.
takeaways: AI self-efficacy acts as a protective factor against job stress when managing cybersecurity responsibilities — developing confidence in AI tools may help employees handle uncertainty more effectively.

Job stress appears to mediate the relationship between uncertainty and cybersecurity behaviour — organisations should address workload and stress levels as part of broader cybersecurity capability-building programmes, not treat training in isolation.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet — full methodology needed to assess sample size, geographic scope, and sector coverage. The theoretical focus on psychological capital and AI as job resource is likely applicable across contexts, but empirical generalisability depends on study design.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams working with AI systems — employees with higher psychological capital may be better positioned to leverage AI as a tool for innovation rather than viewing it as a threat.

Frame AI as a job resource rather than solely a control mechanism — framing influences how workers psychologically respond to algorithm-driven work and their capacity to innovate within those constraints.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample composition, which are not evident from the title and snippet alone. The psychological mechanisms proposed (dual pathways) may apply broadly across knowledge work sectors, but geographic scope and sample characteristics require the full article to assess.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration can boost work engagement through multiple psychological mechanisms — map which pathways (e.g. autonomy, competence, social connection, or cognitive offload) are most active in your team to tailor implementation.

Design AI integration strategies that explicitly address both psychological pathways rather than assuming a single engagement driver — this dual-pathway approach may prevent unintended disengagement in some roles while boosting it in others.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical scope. Generalisability depends on the full article content, which is not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation most likely to be augmented or displaced by AI, then design targeted upskilling interventions before disruption occurs.
Create clear communication about how AI will change work (rather than eliminate it), as uncertainty about job security is a major barrier to employee adoption of new tools.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is broadly applicable, but findings may be limited by sector, organisational size, or geographic scope if not explicitly stated in the full article.
takeaways: Job crafting responses to AI adoption vary based on whether employees perceive AI as an opportunity (approach) versus a threat (avoidance) — tailor change management messaging to reframe AI as enhancing rather than replacing roles to encourage proactive adaptation.

Understanding individual differences in approach-avoidance tendencies allows targeted support: employees with avoidance orientations may need reassurance, upskilling pathways, and early involvement in AI implementation to shift from defensive to constructive job crafting.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis draws on global consulting experience but specific examples and recommendations may reflect biases toward large enterprises and sectors where BCG operates.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption to employees as a workforce capability upgrade, not a replacement threat — this reframing reduces resistance and supports psychological safety during transition.

Design AI transformation programmes that pair upskilling with role redesign; employees are more likely to embrace change when they understand how their work evolves rather than simply adding AI tools to existing jobs.
Identify and engage early adopters within teams to model new AI-enabled workflows — peer-led behaviour change is more persuasive than top-down mandates and builds organisational momentum.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: Framework-level generalisability is high as a conceptual model, but actual applicability depends on context-specific implementation and validation across sectors.
takeaways: The GAP framework (likely Goals, Actions, Processes) provides a structured approach to designing behaviour change interventions — use it as a diagnostic tool to clarify what you're trying to change, how, and why before rolling out workplace initiatives.

Applied behavioural science works best when grounded in clear problem definition and measurement — audit your current behaviour change efforts to identify where goal clarity or process rigour may be lacking.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across multiple sectors and regions, but specific client details and implementation contexts are not disclosed. Findings reflect McKinsey's particular methodology and may not capture all organisational contexts.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling as an organisational change initiative rather than a standalone training program — this positioning increases stakeholder buy-in and integration with broader business transformation efforts.

Design upskilling interventions that address both capability gaps and resistance to change, since technical skills alone won't drive adoption if employees lack psychological readiness or organisational support.

Establish clear accountability and metrics for upskilling outcomes aligned to business outcomes, making the connection between learning investments and measurable performance improvements visible to leadership and participants.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone — no information provided about sample size, geographic scope, sectors studied, or research methodology. Full article needed to assess applicability.
takeaways: DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture are not passive — they actively moderate (strengthen or weaken) how inclusive algorithmic work design affects workplace outcomes, so design AI systems with explicit DEI safeguards rather than assuming fairness is automatic.
Building a diversity-supportive organisational culture is a prerequisite for algorithmic fairness interventions to work effectively; technical fixes alone are insufficient without cultural buy-in.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and size, which cannot be determined from the title and snippet alone. The finding about personality and memory for surprising events may have broad relevance to human cognition, but specific limitations regarding participant demographics, cultural context, and experimental design are unclear.
takeaways: People with different personality traits don't all remember surprising moments the same way — some personality types may encode unexpected events more vividly than others, which is a counterintuitive reminder that memory isn't a universal camera.

The brain treats 'surprise' as a memory enhancer, but your personality acts as a filter that determines how much that boost actually helps you remember — a fascinating interaction between emotion, cognition, and individual differences.
This finding hints at why eyewitness accounts vary so dramatically: it's not just what happened, but who witnessed it and what their personality tends to notice and retain about the unexpected.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — based on a single study with unclear sample size, geography, and methodology; findings may not generalise beyond wine-tasting contexts.
takeaways: AI analysis of casual writing (like wine reviews) can reveal personality traits, suggesting our everyday language and descriptive choices leak information about who we are in unexpected ways.

The connection between how people describe sensory experiences and their personality is surprising because most of us don't think our taste-in-wine reviews are personality assessments — yet an algorithm spotted patterns humans might miss.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — news reports typically synthesize underlying research without full methodological detail; actual scope depends on the original study not described in this snippet.
takeaways: Neuroimaging studies continue to reveal structural or functional brain differences in individuals with psychopathic traits, challenging the notion that personality differences are purely behavioural or learned.

The finding is counterintuitive because it suggests measurable biological markers exist for a personality profile often associated with choice and moral failing — raising fascinating questions about nature vs. nurture in personality development.
This type of research fascinates people because it bridges neuroscience, psychology, and criminology, revealing that even extreme personality traits have a physical substrate in the brain.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Limited — twin study methodology requires genetically identical samples and specific population assumptions; findings may not generalise across different cultural or political contexts.
takeaways: Twin studies suggest authoritarian beliefs have a heritable component, which is counterintuitive since we often think of politics as entirely learned or chosen.
The study highlights how genetics and environment interact to shape political worldviews — nature isn't destiny, but it does load the dice in measurable ways.

This finding is fascinating because it challenges the assumption that 'if only people were educated differently, they'd think differently' — some of the variation runs deeper than socialisation alone.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — large cross-cultural sample suggesting personality-music links transcend geographic and cultural boundaries.
takeaways: Your taste in music reveals surprisingly consistent patterns about your personality across cultures — what appeals to you musically says something universal about who you are.

The finding challenges the idea that music preference is purely cultural; instead, personality appears to be a major driver of whether you gravitate toward rock, classical, pop, or other genres worldwide.
This suggests music could be an unexpectedly simple, culture-blind way to understand personality differences — more intuitive than formal assessments.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from snippet alone — sample size, geographic scope, and study methodology not detailed; this is a summary of research findings rather than the original study.
takeaways: There's a quirky biological angle to personality: thyroid hormones might influence traits like narcissism or callousness, suggesting that some personality variation isn't purely psychological or learned.
The finding highlights an unexpected link between a common endocrine condition and darker interpersonal traits — the kind of counterintuitive result that makes you rethink what drives behaviour.
It's a good reminder that personality and temperament have bodily roots, not just social or experiential ones — fascinating for anyone curious about why people tick the way they do.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings based on academic sector teams; applicability to other organisational contexts and geographic regions unclear from snippet. Results may not generalise to non-academic or less multicultural environments.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to prompt inclusive leadership behaviours; consider how your organisation might use algorithmic prompts or decision-support systems to encourage leaders to actively solicit input from underrepresented team members.

Gendered outcomes in multicultural teams require active intervention — passive diversity without intentional inclusive practices (whether human or AI-supported) is unlikely to improve psychological safety or equity outcomes.
Test whether AI-assisted approaches to leadership (e.g. reminders to check for groupthink, structured input rounds) help your team's leaders notice and correct their own biases in real time.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Broad application across geographies, though sample composition, industry representation, and weighting methodology are not specified in the snippet. Findings likely most relevant to white-collar and professional sectors where PwC operates.
takeaways: Identify which specific workforce concerns (hopes and fears) emerge in your sector and organisation, then design targeted psychological safety interventions to address the top three fears directly rather than generic initiatives.

Use survey data on workforce sentiment to establish a baseline for psychological safety metrics in your organisation, enabling you to track whether interventions meaningfully shift employee perceptions of safety and belonging over time.

Compare your organisation's psychological safety scores against PwC's global benchmarks to pinpoint whether gaps reflect industry norms, local culture, leadership practices, or structural issues requiring different remediation approaches.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — the snippet does not provide sufficient detail on sample size, geographic location, or organisational context. The relationship between AI adoption, psychological safety, and depression requires replication across different cultural and organisational settings to establish broader applicability.
takeaways: AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health when psychological safety is low — prioritise creating a psychologically safe environment during AI implementation by encouraging questions, admitting uncertainty, and protecting employees from blame when navigating AI-related changes.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions — leaders should model transparent decision-making about AI use, explain how AI will affect roles and workflows, and demonstrate commitment to employee wellbeing alongside technological advancement.

Monitor employee psychological outcomes during AI rollouts — track indicators of depression and disengagement, particularly among employees with lower psychological safety, and adjust implementation pace and support accordingly.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG report likely based on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific study design, sample characteristics, and methodological details are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Teams with high psychological safety create more equitable participation, allowing quieter or marginalised voices to contribute without fear of embarrassment or retribution — identify barriers in your team meetings and create explicit norms that invite diverse perspectives.

Psychological safety reduces status-based hierarchies that silence junior staff or underrepresented groups; assess whether your current team dynamics inadvertently discourage contribution from certain members and design interventions (e.g., structured input rounds, anonymous suggestions) to level participation.

articles.title: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Why Employees Aren’t Transparent About Their AI Usage  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — likely reflects patterns in knowledge-work sectors and larger organisations, but geographic scope and sector representation are not detailed. Findings may be more relevant to English-speaking business contexts.
takeaways: Employees hide AI usage when they fear it signals incompetence, laziness, or job insecurity — create explicit permission structures and model transparent AI use yourself to normalise disclosure.

Psychological safety around AI adoption requires separating the act of *using* AI from performance evaluation; clarify which tasks welcome AI assistance and which don't, and reward honesty about tool use over hiding it.
Build feedback loops where employees feel safe reporting AI experiments, failures, and limitations without retaliation — this surfaces risks early and builds trust in AI governance.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — geographic scope and sample characteristics not evident. Findings may be limited to specific industry sectors or organisational contexts with algorithm-driven workflows.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (confidence, hope, resilience, optimism) in teams working with AI systems — employees with stronger psychological capital are more likely to view AI as a resource rather than a threat, enabling innovation rather than resistance.

Design AI implementation programmes that develop employee self-efficacy and optimism about AI capabilities, as psychological capital appears to be a key mediator between AI availability and actual innovative use in the workplace.

Assess and support the psychological readiness of teams before deploying algorithm-driven systems — psychological capital levels may predict which teams will harness AI effectively versus those who will struggle with adoption.
